etymology: Hebrew Serayah, “the LORD is prince,” the chief priest of Jerusalem at the fall of the city, slain at Riblah.
biblical_def: Seraiah was the chief priest of Jerusalem in the last days of the kingdom of Judah, the high priest who served when Nebuchadnezzar broke down the city and burned the temple. When the captain of the guard had taken the city, he took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the keepers of the door (2Ki 25:18; Jer 52:24), and carried them to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where they were put to death. So the last high priest of Solomon’s temple perished, and the old order of the Aaronic priesthood went down into the fire and the sword with the city it served. The dictionary marks Seraiah as the figure of the end of the first temple and its priesthood. The prophet Jeremiah laid the cause of the calamity at the door of the leaders, for the sins of her prophets, and the iniquities of her priests, that have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her (Lam 4:13). Yet the death of the last high priest was not the death of the priesthood, for that office passed to a greater. The Aaronic priests were many, because they were not suffered to continue by reason of death; but this man, Christ, because He continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood (Heb 7:24). Seraiah’s fall is the close of the shadow; the substance abides for ever in the risen Priest who dieth no more.
webster_summary: The chief priest at the fall of Jerusalem, slain at Riblah, in whom the old temple priesthood went down.
webster_full: SERAIAH THE PRIEST, the chief priest at the fall of Jerusalem.
He served when Nebuchadnezzar burned the temple and the city.
He was taken by the captain of the guard to the king at Riblah.
There he was put to death with the second priest and the keepers of the door.
In him the old order of the Aaronic priesthood went down.
scriptures: And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the door:
And the captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, and Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the door:
For the sins of her prophets, and the iniquities of her priests, that have shed the blood of the just in the midst of her,

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; in him the old temple priesthood fell, that the unchangeable priesthood of Christ might be seen.
corruption_paragraphs: Seraiah has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the last high priest of Solomon’s temple, slain at Riblah. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the close of the first temple and its priesthood in the fire of Babylon.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the Aaronic priesthood was a passing shadow whose substance is Christ. The priests of the old order were many, because death suffered them not to continue, and the last of them fell with the city for the sins of the people. But the death of Seraiah was not the death of the priesthood, for that office passed to a greater, who because He continueth ever hath an unchangeable priesthood. The fall of the shadow points the believer to the abiding Priest who dieth no more, in whom the worship of God is established for ever.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the LORD is prince,” Seraiah names the last chief priest of the first temple.

etymology: Hebrew Ebed-melech, “servant of the king,” an Ethiopian eunuch of Zedekiah’s court who rescued Jeremiah.
biblical_def: Ebed-melech was an Ethiopian eunuch in the court of king Zedekiah, a Gentile who feared the God of Israel and showed mercy to His prophet in the day of trouble. When the princes of Judah had cast Jeremiah into a miry dungeon to die of hunger, Ebed-melech went to the king and pleaded for the prophet, saying, These men have done evil in all that they have done to Jeremiah, whom they have cast into the dungeon; and he is like to die for hunger (Jer 38:9). The king bade him take men and draw the prophet up, and he did so with tenderness, putting old rags under Jeremiah’s armholes that the cords might not cut him. For this kindness God sent him a special word of deliverance by the very prophet he had saved: I will surely deliver thee, and thy life shall be for a prey unto thee, because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD (Jer 39:18). The dictionary marks Ebed-melech as the Gentile who feared God and helped His servant, and was rewarded for his faith. His deliverance fulfils the Lord’s own word, that whosoever gives a cup of cold water to a disciple shall in no wise lose his reward (Mat 10:42); for God is not unrighteous to forget the labour of love shewn toward His name (Heb 6:10). He stands as a witness that grace is no respecter of nation, and that kindness to God’s afflicted servants is remembered in heaven.
webster_summary: An Ethiopian eunuch of Zedekiah’s court who rescued Jeremiah and was delivered for his trust in God.
webster_full: EBED-MELECH, an Ethiopian eunuch in the court of king Zedekiah.

scriptures: For I will surely deliver thee, and thou shalt not fall by the sword, but thy life shall be for a prey unto thee: because thou hast put thy trust in me, saith the LORD.

And whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, verily I say unto you, he shall in no wise lose his reward.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the Gentile who feared God and helped His prophet, and was delivered for his trust.
corruption_paragraphs: Ebed-melech has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Ethiopian who saved Jeremiah from the dungeon. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the mercy of a God-fearing Gentile to the afflicted prophet, and the reward God gave it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: that grace is no respecter of nation, and that kindness to God’s afflicted servants is remembered in heaven. Ebed-melech was a Gentile and a eunuch, yet he feared the God of Israel and risked the king’s court to save His prophet; and God sent him a word of deliverance because he had put his trust in the LORD. The Lord Jesus confirms the principle: whosoever gives a cup of cold water to a disciple shall not lose his reward, for God is not unrighteous to forget the labour of love shewn toward His name.

etymology: Hebrew Baruk, “blessed,” the son of Neriah, the faithful scribe and companion of Jeremiah.
biblical_def: Baruch the son of Neriah was the faithful scribe and companion of the prophet Jeremiah, who shared his master’s reproach through the long sorrowful years before and during the fall of Jerusalem. It was Baruch who wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD upon a roll of a book (Jer 36:4), and who read them aloud in the temple at the peril of his life when the prophet was shut up; and when the king burned the roll, Baruch wrote it again. The labour was hard and the times were dark, and Baruch was tempted to despair, crying, Woe is me now! for the LORD hath added grief to my sorrow; I fainted in my sighing, and I find no rest (Jer 45:3). To him the LORD sent a searching and tender word: And seekest thou great things for thyself? seek them not; but thy life will I give unto thee for a prey in all places whither thou goest (Jer 45:5). The dictionary marks Baruch as the pattern of faithful service in a hard time, who sought not great things for himself but was content to write and to suffer beside the prophet of God. His example presses home that it is required in stewards that a man be found faithful (1Co 4:2); and his preserved roll is a witness that the word of God, written by His servants and burned by His enemies, cannot be destroyed.
webster_summary: The faithful scribe of Jeremiah, who wrote the prophet’s words and was bidden to seek not great things for himself.
webster_full: BARUCH THE SCRIBE, the son of Neriah and companion of Jeremiah.
He wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah the words of the LORD upon a roll.
He read them in the temple at the peril of his life.
When the king burned the roll, he wrote it again.
He was bidden to seek not great things for himself.
scriptures: Then Jeremiah called Baruch the son of Neriah: and Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah all the words of the LORD, which he had spoken unto him, upon a roll of a book.

And seekest thou great things for thyself? seek them not: for, behold, I will bring evil upon all flesh, saith the LORD: but thy life will I give unto thee for a prey in all places whither thou goest.
Thou didst say, Woe is me now! for the LORD hath added grief to my sorrow; I fainted in my sighing, and I find no rest.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the faithful scribe content to serve and suffer beside the prophet, seeking not great things for himself.
corruption_paragraphs: Baruch has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the faithful scribe who wrote and preserved the words of Jeremiah. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark his contentment in a hard and unrewarded service.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faithful service in a dark time, content to seek not great things for oneself. Baruch was tempted to despair under the grief of his labour, and the LORD met him not with promise of greatness but with a charge to seek it not, and the gift of his life for a prey. So the steward of God is taught that it is required of him to be found faithful, not famous; and Baruch’s preserved roll, written by a servant and burned by a king yet written again, is a standing witness that the word of God cannot be destroyed by the enemies who hate it.

etymology: Hebrew Gedalyah, “the LORD is great,” the godly governor of Judah set over the remnant after the fall of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Gedaliah the son of Ahikam was a godly man of Judah whom the king of Babylon set as governor over the poor remnant left in the land after Jerusalem fell. He sought to gather the scattered people and to settle them in peace, swearing to them, Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you (2Ki 25:24). But there was treachery in the camp. Johanan warned him that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah was sent by the king of the Ammonites to slay him; but Gedaliah, gentle and unsuspecting, believed them not (Jer 40:14). And Ishmael arose and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam with the sword, and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land (Jer 41:2), feasting at his table and then murdering his host. The dictionary marks Gedaliah as the good ruler treacherously slain, whose death scattered the last hope of the remnant in the land. His murder, by one who ate of his bread and lifted up his heel against him (Psa 41:9), is a dark picture of the treachery that strikes down the faithful; and his too-trusting gentleness is a quiet warning that even goodness must be wise, and that the godly are not to despise the warning of danger, but to walk in the wisdom that is from above.
webster_summary: The godly governor of Judah’s remnant after the fall, treacherously murdered by Ishmael.
webster_full: GEDALIAH THE GOVERNOR, set over the remnant of Judah after the fall.
He was the son of Ahikam, a godly and gentle ruler.
He sought to settle the people in peace under Babylon.
He disbelieved the warning of Ishmael’s plot against him.
Ishmael feasted at his table and then slew him.
scriptures: And Gedaliah sware to them, and to their men, and said unto them, Fear not to be the servants of the Chaldees: dwell in the land, and serve the king of Babylon; and it shall be well with you.

Then arose Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, and the ten men that were with him, and smote Gedaliah the son of Ahikam the son of Shaphan with the sword, and slew him, whom the king of Babylon had made governor over the land.
And said unto him, Dost thou certainly know that Baalis the king of the Ammonites hath sent Ishmael the son of Nethaniah to slay thee? But Gedaliah the son of Ahikam believed them not.
Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the good ruler treacherously slain, a warning that even goodness must walk in wisdom.
corruption_paragraphs: Gedaliah has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the godly governor murdered by Ishmael. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the treachery that struck down the last hope of the remnant in the land.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is twofold: the wickedness of treachery against the faithful, and the wisdom that even goodness must keep. Ishmael ate of Gedaliah’s bread and then lifted up his heel against him, a dark figure of the betrayal that David and the Lord Himself foretold. Yet the dictionary marks also that Gedaliah, gentle and good, despised the warning of his danger and believed not, and so fell. The godly are not to be suspicious in heart, but neither are they to be simple; for goodness must be joined to the wisdom that is from above, lest mercy be undone by want of discernment.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the LORD is great,” Gedaliah names the godly governor of Judah’s remnant.

He was treacherously slain at his own table.
usage: Like Gedaliah, the good ruler may fall to treachery he was too gentle to suspect.

etymology: Hebrew Yohanan, “the LORD is gracious,” a captain of the remnant of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem.
biblical_def: Johanan the son of Kareah was a captain of the forces of the remnant of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem, who began well but ended in disobedience. He warned the godly governor Gedaliah of Ishmael’s plot, and when Gedaliah was slain, Johanan pursued and rescued the captives Ishmael had taken. Then, fearing the wrath of Babylon, he and the people came to Jeremiah and asked him to enquire of the LORD their way, vowing, Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God (Jer 42:6). The prophet brought God’s plain answer: abide in the land and fear not; go ye not into Egypt (Jer 42:19). But Johanan and the captains would not believe it, and they took all the remnant, and Jeremiah with them, and came into the land of Egypt, for they obeyed not the voice of the LORD (Jer 43:7). The dictionary marks Johanan as the man who sought God’s counsel and then refused it, who walked down into Egypt having vowed to obey. His fall is a solemn warning against asking the will of God with a heart already set on its own way, and against fleeing to Egypt, the figure of the world’s help, by men who have not asked at God’s mouth, but strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh (Isa 30:2).
webster_summary: A captain of Judah’s remnant who sought God’s counsel through Jeremiah and then disobeyed, leading the people into Egypt.
webster_full: JOHANAN THE SON OF KAREAH, a captain of Judah’s remnant after the fall.
He warned Gedaliah of Ishmael’s plot and rescued the captives.
He asked Jeremiah to enquire of the LORD, vowing to obey.
God commanded them to abide in the land and not go to Egypt.
He disobeyed and led the remnant down into Egypt.
scriptures: Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey the voice of the LORD our God, to whom we send thee; that it may be well with us, when we obey the voice of the LORD our God.
The LORD hath said concerning you, O ye remnant of Judah; Go ye not into Egypt: know certainly that I have admonished you this day.
So they came into the land of Egypt: for they obeyed not the voice of the LORD: thus came they even to Tahpanhes.
That walk to go down into Egypt, and have not asked at my mouth; to strengthen themselves in the strength of Pharaoh, and to trust in the shadow of Egypt!
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the man who sought God’s counsel and refused it, a warning against asking with a heart already set.
corruption_paragraphs: Johanan has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the captain who led the remnant into Egypt against God’s word. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the danger of seeking the will of God with a heart already resolved on its own way.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the folly of asking God’s counsel without meaning to obey it. Johanan and the people vowed to obey whatever the LORD should say, good or evil; but when the answer crossed their fears, they would not believe it, and went down into Egypt. So men still seek divine sanction for a course already chosen, and call it the will of God. The flight to Egypt is the figure of every refuge sought in the world’s strength by those who have not truly asked at God’s mouth; and Johanan’s disobedience warns that a vow of obedience is worthless where the heart is set upon its own way.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew for “the LORD is gracious,” Johanan names the captain who led the remnant into Egypt.

etymology: Hebrew Ahiqam, “my brother hath risen,” a prince of Judah who shielded Jeremiah from death.
biblical_def: Ahikam the son of Shaphan was a prince of Judah in the days of Josiah and his sons, a man who used his place and influence to protect the prophet of God. When Jeremiah had preached judgment upon the temple and the city, and the priests and the people sought his death, the hand of Ahikam the son of Shaphan was with Jeremiah, that they should not give him into the hand of the people to put him to death (Jer 26:24). By his courage and standing the prophet was spared to continue his ministry. Ahikam was also the father of Gedaliah, the godly governor of the remnant; so the house of Shaphan was a house of friends to the word of God in an evil time. The dictionary marks Ahikam as the man who shielded God’s servant when the crowd cried for his blood, fulfilling the wise man’s charge to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and those that are ready to be slain (Pro 24:11). Such kindness to a persecuted prophet is reckoned by the Lord as done unto Himself, for inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me (Mat 25:40). Ahikam teaches that those whom God has set in places of influence are to use them to remember them that are in bonds, and to stand between the faithful and the rage of their enemies.
webster_summary: A prince of Judah who used his influence to protect Jeremiah from being put to death.

corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the man who used his influence to shield God’s servant from the rage of the crowd.
corruption_paragraphs: Ahikam has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the prince who saved Jeremiah from death. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the use of place and influence to protect the persecuted servant of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that those whom God sets in places of influence are to use them to shield the faithful from the rage of their enemies. The hand of Ahikam was with Jeremiah, and the prophet was spared; and such kindness to a persecuted servant of God is reckoned by the Lord as done unto Himself. The believer is bidden to deliver them that are drawn unto death, and to remember them that are in bonds as bound with them. Ahikam teaches that worldly standing is well spent when it is spent to stand between the faithful and those who seek their blood.

etymology: Hebrew Yahaziel, “God sees,” a Levite of the sons of Asaph on whom the Spirit of the LORD came before Jehoshaphat’s battle.
biblical_def: Jahaziel was a Levite of the sons of Asaph upon whom the Spirit of the LORD came in the midst of the congregation, when king Jehoshaphat and all Judah stood before the house of God in fear of a great invading multitude. Through him God spoke a word that has heartened His people in every battle since: Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s (2Ch 20:15). He bade them, Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD with you (2Ch 20:17); and on the morrow, as Judah went out singing the praises of God, the LORD set ambushments against the enemy and they destroyed one another. The dictionary marks Jahaziel as the herald of the truth that the LORD fights for His people. His word is one with the word of Moses at the Red Sea, The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace (Exo 14:14), and with the psalm, Be still, and know that I am God (Psa 46:10). He teaches the church that her warfare is the LORD’s, that the victory is won not by her strength but by His, and that the posture of faith in the day of overwhelming odds is to stand still, to praise, and to see the salvation of God.
webster_summary: A Levite on whom the Spirit came, who told Jehoshaphat the battle was not his but God’s.
webster_full: JAHAZIEL THE LEVITE, a Levite of the sons of Asaph.

He declared that the battle is not Judah’s but God’s.
He bade them stand still and see the salvation of the LORD.
Judah went out singing, and the LORD destroyed the enemy.
scriptures: And he said, Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat, Thus saith the LORD unto you, Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s.

Ye shall not need to fight in this battle: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD with you, O Judah and Jerusalem: fear not, nor be dismayed; to morrow go out against them: for the LORD will be with you.

corruption_paragraphs: Jahaziel has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the Levite who spoke God’s word of deliverance before Jehoshaphat’s battle. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the truth he was given to declare, that the battle is the LORD’s.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD fights for His people, and that the posture of faith in the day of overwhelming odds is to stand still and see His salvation. Jahaziel’s word is one with the word at the Red Sea and with the psalm, Be still, and know that I am God. The church’s warfare is the LORD’s; her victory is won not by her strength but by His, and is often gained as she goes out praising rather than fighting. So the believer, faced with a great multitude, is taught not to faint but to trust, for the battle is not his, but God’s.

etymology: Hebrew Oded, perhaps “restorer” or “he hath set up,” a prophet of the LORD in Samaria in the days of king Ahaz.
biblical_def: Oded was a prophet of the LORD in Samaria in the days of Ahaz king of Judah, when the army of the northern kingdom returned from war with a great host of captives, men, women, and children of their brethren of Judah, whom they meant to make bondmen. Oded went out before the host and rebuked them, saying that though the LORD had indeed delivered Judah into their hand because of His wrath, yet they had slain them in a rage that reacheth up unto heaven (2Ch 28:9), and now purposed to enslave their own brethren. Therefore he charged them, Now hear me, and deliver the captives again, which ye have taken captive of your brethren: for the fierce wrath of the LORD is upon you (2Ch 28:11). And the word prevailed: the captives were clothed, shod, fed, and carried back to their own people. The dictionary marks Oded as the prophet of mercy to the brethren, whose bold word turned an army from cruelty to compassion. His rebuke embodies the prophet Micah’s charge, to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God (Mic 6:8), and the apostle’s warning that he shall have judgment without mercy that hath shewed no mercy, and that mercy rejoiceth against judgment (Jas 2:13). He teaches that victory is no licence for cruelty, and that the people of God are to temper power with mercy toward their own.
webster_summary: A prophet of Samaria who turned the army of Israel from enslaving their Judahite captives to mercy.
webster_full: ODED THE PROPHET, a prophet of the LORD in Samaria under king Ahaz.
The army of Israel returned with captives of their brethren of Judah.
Oded went out and rebuked them for their cruelty and rage.
He charged them to deliver the captives again.
The captives were clothed, fed, and carried back to their people.
scriptures: But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded: and he went out before the host that came to Samaria, and said unto them, Behold, because the LORD God of your fathers was wroth with Judah, he hath delivered them into your hand, and ye have slain them in a rage that reacheth up unto heaven.
Now hear me therefore, and deliver the captives again, which ye have taken captive of your brethren: for the fierce wrath of the LORD is upon you.
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
For he shall have judgment without mercy, that hath shewed no mercy; and mercy rejoiceth against judgment.
corruption_summary: A figure of Scripture; the prophet whose bold word turned an army from cruelty to mercy toward their brethren.
corruption_paragraphs: Oded has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as the prophet who turned the army of Israel from enslaving their captive brethren. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the power of a bold word of God to turn cruelty into compassion.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that victory is no licence for cruelty, and that the people of God are to temper power with mercy. The men of Israel had been the LORD’s rod against Judah, yet they slew in a rage that reached up to heaven and would have enslaved their own brethren; and Oded warned that the fierce wrath of the LORD was upon them for it. His rebuke embodies the requirement to do justly, and to love mercy; for he shall have judgment without mercy that hath shewed no mercy, and mercy rejoiceth against judgment. The dictionary honours the prophet who taught a conquering army to remember its brethren and to fear the God who sees.

etymology: From the common Roman name Gaius, borne by a host of the apostle Paul and a beloved friend of the apostle John.
biblical_def: Gaius is a name borne by more than one believer in the New Testament, chiefly remembered as a host and helper of the apostles. At Corinth there was a Gaius whom Paul himself baptized, and who became the apostle’s host and a host of the whole church, opening his house to the gathered saints; Paul sends his greeting in the Epistle to the Romans, Gaius mine host, and of the whole church, saluteth you (Rom 16:23), and names him among the few he baptized with his own hand (1Co 1:14). And the apostle John wrote his third epistle to a beloved Gaius, commending him for his faithful hospitality to the travelling preachers of the gospel: Beloved, thou doest faithfully whatsoever thou doest to the brethren, and to strangers (3Jo 1:5), adding that we ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth (3Jo 1:8). The dictionary marks Gaius as the pattern of Christian hospitality, the open house and open heart that receive the servants of Christ and so share in their labour. Whether the Corinthian host of Paul or the beloved of John, the men who bore this name are honoured for ministering to the saints; and they teach that to lodge and help the messengers of the gospel is itself a fellowship in the truth they carry, and a service the Lord remembers.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the grace of Christian hospitality, the open house and open heart that receive the servants of Christ. Gaius of Corinth was host to the whole church; the beloved Gaius of John’s epistle dealt faithfully with the brethren and with strangers, lodging the travelling preachers of the gospel. The apostle teaches that we ought to receive such, that we might be fellowhelpers to the truth; for to lodge and help the messengers of the gospel is itself a fellowship in the truth they carry. The men named Gaius teach the church that hospitality to the saints is no small service, but a sharing in their labour that the Lord remembers.

etymology: From the Latin Pudens, “modest” or “bashful,” a Christian of Rome who sent greeting to Timothy through the apostle Paul.
biblical_def: Pudens was a Christian of Rome named among the few who stood by the apostle Paul in the city in his last imprisonment, and who joined in sending greeting to Timothy. In the closing lines of his last epistle, written as he awaited death, Paul wrote, Do thy diligence to come before winter. Eubulus greeteth thee, and Pudens, and Linus, and Claudia, and all the brethren (2Ti 4:21). These were the saints of the Roman church who did not forsake the apostle when many had fled, and whose names the Spirit was pleased to set down for ever in the Scripture. Of Pudens himself little more is known, yet his name stands in the record of those who were of Caesar’s household and city and yet belonged to Christ, for there were saints even in the household of Caesar (Php 4:22). The dictionary marks Pudens among the lesser-known saints whose faithfulness in a hard place and a dark hour is honoured by their bare mention in the word of God. When no man stood with Paul at his first answer, yet the Lord stood with him (2Ti 4:17); and the brethren named with Pudens are a witness that even in persecuting Rome the Lord had a people who would not be ashamed of His servant in chains. Their love teaches that brotherly love should continue (Heb 13:1), and that to stand by the persecuted is to be remembered with them in heaven.
webster_summary: A Christian of Rome who, with Linus and Claudia, sent greeting to Timothy in Paul’s last epistle.

corruption_paragraphs: Pudens has drawn no redefinition from the present age, surviving as a name in the closing greetings of Paul’s last epistle. The dictionary records him that the reader may mark the saints of Rome who did not forsake the apostle in his chains.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the honour God puts upon the lesser-known saints whose faithfulness in a hard place is recorded by the bare mention of their names. When many had fled and no man stood with Paul at his first answer, the Lord stood with him, and a faithful few, Pudens among them, stood also. They were of the city and perhaps the household of Caesar, yet they belonged to Christ, for there were saints even in Caesar’s household. Their love teaches that brotherly love should continue, and that to stand by the persecuted servant of God in a dark hour is to be remembered with him for ever in the word and in heaven.
